# Navigation Overview
  * 05/06/2025


Feedback
Windows Presentation Foundation (WPF) supports browser-style navigation that can be used in two types of applications: standalone applications and XAML browser applications (XBAPs). To package content for navigation, WPF provides the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) class. You can navigate from one [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) to another declaratively, by using a [Hyperlink](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.documents.hyperlink), or programmatically, by using the [NavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice). WPF uses the journal to remember pages that have been navigated from and to navigate back to them.
[Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page), [Hyperlink](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.documents.hyperlink), [NavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice), and the journal form the core of the navigation support offered by WPF. This overview explores these features in detail before covering advanced navigation support that includes navigation to loose Extensible Application Markup Language (XAML) files, HTML files, and objects.
In this topic, the term "browser" refers only to browsers that can host WPF applications, which currently includes Microsoft Internet Explorer and Firefox. Where specific WPF features are supported only by a particular browser, the browser version is referred to.
## Navigation in WPF Applications
This topic provides an overview of the key navigation capabilities in WPF. These capabilities are available to both standalone applications and XBAPs, although this topic presents them within the context of an XBAP.
This topic doesn't discuss how to build and deploy XBAPs. For more information on XBAPs, see [WPF XAML Browser Applications Overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/wpf-xaml-browser-applications-overview).
This section explains and demonstrates the following aspects of navigation:
  * [Implementing a Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/navigation-overview#CreatingAXAMLPage)
  * [Configuring a Start Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/navigation-overview#Configuring_a_Start_Page)
  * [Configuring the Host Window's Title, Width, and Height](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/navigation-overview#ConfiguringAXAMLPage)
  * [Hyperlink Navigation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/navigation-overview#NavigatingBetweenXAMLPages)
  * [Fragment Navigation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/navigation-overview#FragmentNavigation)
  * [Navigation Service](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/navigation-overview#NavigationService)
  * [Programmatic Navigation with the Navigation Service](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/navigation-overview#Programmatic_Navigation_with_the_Navigation_Service)
  * [Navigation Lifetime](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/navigation-overview#Navigation_Lifetime)
  * [Remembering Navigation with the Journal](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/navigation-overview#NavigationHistory)
  * [Page Lifetime and the Journal](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/navigation-overview#PageLifetime)
  * [Retaining Content State with Navigation History](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/navigation-overview#RetainingContentStateWithNavigationHistory)
  * [Cookies](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/navigation-overview#Cookies)
  * [Structured Navigation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/navigation-overview#Structured_Navigation)


### Implementing a Page
In WPF, you can navigate to several content types that include .NET Framework objects, custom objects, enumeration values, user controls, XAML files, and HTML files. However, you'll find that the most common and convenient way to package content is by using [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page). Furthermore, [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) implements navigation-specific features to enhance their appearance and simplify development.
Using [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page), you can declaratively implement a navigable page of XAML content by using markup like the following.
XAML Copy
```
<Page xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation" />

```

A [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) that is implemented in XAML markup has `Page` as its root element and requires the WPF XML namespace declaration. The `Page` element contains the content that you want to navigate to and display. You add content by setting the `Page.Content` property element, as shown in the following markup.
XAML Copy
```
<Page xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation">
  <Page.Content>
    <!-- Page Content -->
    Hello, Page!
  </Page.Content>
</Page>

```

`Page.Content` can only contain one child element; in the preceding example, the content is a single string, "Hello, Page!" In practice, you will usually use a layout control as the child element (see [Layout](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/advanced/layout)) to contain and compose your content.
The child elements of a `Page` element are considered to be the content of a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) and, consequently, you don't need to use the explicit `Page.Content` declaration. The following markup is the declarative equivalent to the preceding sample.
XAML Copy
```
<Page xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation">
  <!-- Page Content -->
  Hello, Page!
</Page>

```

In this case, `Page.Content` is automatically set with the child elements of the `Page` element. For more information, see [WPF Content Model](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/controls/wpf-content-model).
A markup-only [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) is useful for displaying content. However, a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) can also display controls that allow users to interact with the page, and it can respond to user interaction by handling events and calling application logic. An interactive [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) is implemented by using a combination of markup and code-behind, as shown in the following example.
XAML Copy
```
<Page
    xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
    xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
    x:Class="SDKSample.HomePage">
  Hello, from the XBAP HomePage!
</Page>

```

C# Copy
```
using System.Windows.Controls;

namespace SDKSample
{
    public partial class HomePage : Page
    {
        public HomePage(
        {
            InitializeComponent();
        }
    }
}

```
```

Imports System.Windows.Controls

Namespace SDKSample
    Partial Public Class HomePage
        Inherits Page
        Public Sub New()
            InitializeComponent()
        End Sub
    End Class
End Namespace

```

To allow a markup file and code-behind file to work together, the following configuration is required:
  * In markup, the `Page` element must include the `x:Class` attribute. When the application is built, the existence of `x:Class` in the markup file causes Microsoft build engine (MSBuild) to create a `partial` class that derives from [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) and has the name that is specified by the `x:Class` attribute. This requires the addition of an XML namespace declaration for the XAML schema ( `xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"` ). The generated `partial` class implements `InitializeComponent`, which is called to register the events and set the properties that are implemented in markup.
  * In code-behind, the class must be a `partial` class with the same name that is specified by the `x:Class` attribute in markup, and it must derive from [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page). This allows the code-behind file to be associated with the `partial` class that is generated for the markup file when the application is built (see [Building a WPF Application](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/building-a-wpf-application-wpf)).
  * In code-behind, the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) class must implement a constructor that calls the `InitializeComponent` method. `InitializeComponent` is implemented by the markup file's generated `partial` class to register events and set properties that are defined in markup.


When you add a new [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) to your project using Visual Studio, the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) is implemented using both markup and code-behind, and it includes the necessary configuration to create the association between the markup and code-behind files as described here.
Once you have a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page), you can navigate to it. To specify the first [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) that an application navigates to, you need to configure the start [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page).
### Configuring a Start Page
XBAPs require a certain amount of application infrastructure to be hosted in a browser. In WPF, the [Application](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application) class is part of an application definition that establishes the required application infrastructure (see [Application Management Overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/application-management-overview)).
An application definition is usually implemented using both markup and code-behind, with the markup file configured as an MSBuild`ApplicationDefinition` item. The following is an application definition for an XBAP.
XAML Copy
```
<Application
    xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
    xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
    x:Class="SDKSample.App" />

```

C# Copy
```
using System.Windows;

namespace SDKSample
{
    public partial class App : Application { }
}

```
```

Imports System.Windows

Namespace SDKSample
    Partial Public Class App
        Inherits Application
    End Class
End Namespace

```

An XBAP can use its application definition to specify a start [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page), which is the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) that is automatically loaded when the XBAP is launched. You do this by setting the [StartupUri](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application.startupuri) property with the uniform resource identifier (URI) for the desired [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page).
In most cases, the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) is either compiled into or deployed with an application. In these cases, the URI that identifies a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) is a pack URI, which is a URI that conforms to the _pack_ scheme. Pack URIs are discussed further in [Pack URIs in WPF](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/pack-uris-in-wpf). You can also navigate to content using the http scheme, which is discussed below.
You can set [StartupUri](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application.startupuri) declaratively in markup, as shown in the following example.
XAML Copy
```
<Application
    xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
    xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
    x:Class="SDKSample.App"
    StartupUri="PageWithHyperlink.xaml" />

```

In this example, the `StartupUri` attribute is set with a relative pack URI that identifies HomePage.xaml. When the XBAP is launched, HomePage.xaml is automatically navigated to and displayed. This is demonstrated by the following figure, which shows an XBAP that was launched from a Web server.
For more information regarding the development and deployment of XBAPs, see [WPF XAML Browser Applications Overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/wpf-xaml-browser-applications-overview) and [Deploying a WPF Application](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/deploying-a-wpf-application-wpf).
### Configuring the Host Window's Title, Width, and Height
One thing you may have noticed from the previous figure is that the title of both the browser and the tab panel is the URI for the XBAP. Besides being long, the title is neither attractive nor informative. For this reason, [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) offers a way for you to change the title by setting the [WindowTitle](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page.windowtitle) property. Furthermore, you can configure the width and height of the browser window by setting [WindowWidth](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page.windowwidth) and [WindowHeight](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page.windowheight), respectively.
[WindowTitle](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page.windowtitle), [WindowWidth](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page.windowwidth), and [WindowHeight](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page.windowheight) can be set declaratively in markup, as shown in the following example.
XAML Copy
```
<Page
    xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
    xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
    x:Class="SDKSample.HomePage"
    WindowTitle="Page Title"
    WindowWidth="500"
    WindowHeight="200">
  Hello, from the XBAP HomePage!
</Page>

```

The result is shown in the following figure.
### Hyperlink Navigation
A typical XBAP comprises several pages. The simplest way to navigate from one page to another is to use a [Hyperlink](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.documents.hyperlink). You can declaratively add a [Hyperlink](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.documents.hyperlink) to a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) by using the `Hyperlink` element, which is shown in the following markup.
XAML Copy
```
<Page
  xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
  WindowTitle="Page With Hyperlink"
  WindowWidth="250"
  WindowHeight="250">

```

XAML Copy
```
<Hyperlink NavigateUri="UriOfPageToNavigateTo.xaml">
  Navigate to Another Page
</Hyperlink>

```

XAML Copy
```
</Page>

```

A `Hyperlink` element requires the following:
  * The pack URI of the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) to navigate to, as specified by the `NavigateUri` attribute.
  * Content that a user can click to initiate the navigation, such as text and images (for the content that the `Hyperlink` element can contain, see [Hyperlink](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.documents.hyperlink)).


The following figure shows an XBAP with a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) that has a [Hyperlink](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.documents.hyperlink).
As you would expect, clicking the [Hyperlink](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.documents.hyperlink) causes the XBAP to navigate to the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) that is identified by the `NavigateUri` attribute. Additionally, the XBAP adds an entry for the previous [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) to the Recent Pages list in Internet Explorer. This is shown in the following figure.
As well as supporting navigation from one [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) to another, [Hyperlink](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.documents.hyperlink) also supports fragment navigation.
### Fragment Navigation
_Fragment navigation_ is the navigation to a content fragment in either the current [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) or another [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page). In WPF, a content fragment is the content that is contained by a named element. A named element is an element that has its `Name` attribute set. The following markup shows a named `TextBlock` element that contains a content fragment.
XAML Copy
```
<Page
    xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
    WindowTitle="Page With Fragments" >

```

XAML Copy
```
<!-- Content Fragment called "Fragment1" -->
<TextBlock Name="Fragment1">
  Ea vel dignissim te aliquam facilisis ...
</TextBlock>

```

XAML Copy
```
</Page>

```

For a [Hyperlink](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.documents.hyperlink) to navigate to a content fragment, the `NavigateUri` attribute must include the following:
  * The URI of the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) with the content fragment to navigate to.
  * A "#" character.
  * The name of the element on the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) that contains the content fragment.


A fragment URI has the following format.
_PageURI_ `#` _ElementName_
The following shows an example of a `Hyperlink` that is configured to navigate to a content fragment.
XAML Copy
```
<Page
  xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
  WindowTitle="Page That Navigates To Fragment" >

```

XAML Copy
```
<Hyperlink NavigateUri="PageWithFragments.xaml#Fragment1">
  Navigate To pack Fragment
</Hyperlink>

```

XAML Copy
```
</Page>

```

This section describes the default fragment navigation implementation in WPF. WPF also allows you to implement your own fragment navigation scheme which, in part, requires handling the [NavigationService.FragmentNavigation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.fragmentnavigation#system-windows-navigation-navigationservice-fragmentnavigation) event.
You can navigate to fragments in loose XAML pages (markup-only XAML files with `Page` as the root element) only if the pages can be browsed via HTTP.
However, a loose XAML page can navigate to its own fragments.
### Navigation Service
While [Hyperlink](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.documents.hyperlink) allows a user to initiate navigation to a particular [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page), the work of locating and downloading the page is performed by the [NavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice) class. Essentially, [NavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice) provides the ability to process a navigation request on behalf of client code, such as the [Hyperlink](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.documents.hyperlink). Additionally, [NavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice) implements higher-level support for tracking and influencing a navigation request.
When a [Hyperlink](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.documents.hyperlink) is clicked, WPF calls [NavigationService.Navigate](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.navigate) to locate and download the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) at the specified pack URI. The downloaded [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) is converted to a tree of objects whose root object is an instance of the downloaded [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page). A reference to the root [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) object is stored in the [NavigationService.Content](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.content) property. The pack URI for the content that was navigated to is stored in the [NavigationService.Source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.source) property, while the [NavigationService.CurrentSource](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.currentsource) stores the pack URI for the last page that was navigated to.
It is possible for a WPF application to have more than one currently active [NavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice). For more information, see [Navigation Hosts](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/navigation-overview#Navigation_Hosts) later in this topic.
### Programmatic Navigation with the Navigation Service
You don't need to know about [NavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice) if navigation is implemented declaratively in markup using [Hyperlink](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.documents.hyperlink), because [Hyperlink](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.documents.hyperlink) uses the [NavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice) on your behalf. This means that, as long as either the direct or indirect parent of a [Hyperlink](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.documents.hyperlink) is a navigation host (see [Navigation Hosts](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/navigation-overview#Navigation_Hosts)), [Hyperlink](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.documents.hyperlink) will be able to find and use the navigation host's navigation service to process a navigation request.
However, there are situations when you need to use [NavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice) directly, including the following:
  * When you need to instantiate a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) using a non-parameterless constructor.
  * When you need to set properties on the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) before you navigate to it.
  * When the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) that needs to be navigated to can only be determined at run time.


In these situations, you need to write code to programmatically initiate navigation by calling the [Navigate](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.navigate) method of the [NavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice) object. That requires getting a reference to a [NavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice).
#### Getting a Reference to the NavigationService
For reasons that are covered in the [Navigation Hosts](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/navigation-overview#Navigation_Hosts) section, a WPF application can have more than one [NavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice). This means that your code needs a way to find a [NavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice), which is usually the [NavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice) that navigated to the current [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page). You can get a reference to a [NavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice) by calling the `static`[NavigationService.GetNavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.getnavigationservice) method. To get the [NavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice) that navigated to a particular [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page), you pass a reference to the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) as the argument of the [GetNavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.getnavigationservice) method. The following code shows how to get the [NavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice) for the current [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page).

```
using System.Windows.Navigation;

```

C# Copy
```
// Get a reference to the NavigationService that navigated to this Page
NavigationService ns = NavigationService.GetNavigationService(this);

```
```
' Get a reference to the NavigationService that navigated to this Page
Dim ns As NavigationService = NavigationService.GetNavigationService(Me)

```

#### Programmatic Navigation with a Pack URI
If you need to construct a pack URI programmatically (when you can only determine the pack URI at run time, for example), you can use the [NavigationService.Navigate](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.navigate) method. This is shown in the following example.
XAML Copy
```
<Page
    xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
    xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
    x:Class="SDKSample.NSUriNavigationPage">
  <Hyperlink Click="hyperlink_Click">Navigate to Page by Pack URI</Hyperlink>
</Page>

```

C# Copy
```
using System;
using System.Windows;
using System.Windows.Controls;
using System.Windows.Navigation;

namespace SDKSample
{
    public partial class NSUriNavigationPage : Page
    {
        public NSUriNavigationPage(
        {
            InitializeComponent();
        }

        void hyperlink_Click(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
        {
            // Create a pack URI
            Uri uri = new Uri("AnotherPage.xaml", UriKind.Relative);

            // Get the navigation service that was used to
            // navigate to this page, and navigate to
            // AnotherPage.xaml
            this.NavigationService.Navigate(uri);
        }
    }
}

### Navigation Lifetime
There are many ways to initiate navigation, as you've seen. When navigation is initiated, and while navigation is in progress, you can track and influence the navigation using the following events that are implemented by [NavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice):
  * [Navigating](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.navigating#system-windows-navigation-navigationservice-navigating). Occurs when a new navigation is requested. Can be used to cancel the navigation.
  * [NavigationProgress](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.navigationprogress#system-windows-navigation-navigationservice-navigationprogress). Occurs periodically during a download to provide navigation progress information.
  * [Navigated](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.navigated#system-windows-navigation-navigationservice-navigated). Occurs when the page has been located and downloaded.
  * [NavigationStopped](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.navigationstopped#system-windows-navigation-navigationservice-navigationstopped). Occurs when the navigation is stopped (by calling [StopLoading](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.stoploading)), or when a new navigation is requested while a current navigation is in progress.
  * [NavigationFailed](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.navigationfailed#system-windows-navigation-navigationservice-navigationfailed). Occurs when an error is raised while navigating to the requested content.
  * [LoadCompleted](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.loadcompleted#system-windows-navigation-navigationservice-loadcompleted). Occurs when content that was navigated to is loaded and parsed, and has begun rendering.
  * [FragmentNavigation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.fragmentnavigation#system-windows-navigation-navigationservice-fragmentnavigation). Occurs when navigation to a content fragment begins, which happens:
    * Immediately, if the desired fragment is in the current content.
    * After the source content has been loaded, if the desired fragment is in different content.


The navigation events are raised in the order that is illustrated by the following figure.
In general, a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) isn't concerned about these events. It is more likely that an application is concerned with them and, for that reason, these events are also raised by the [Application](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application) class:
  * [Application.Navigating](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application.navigating#system-windows-application-navigating)
  * [Application.NavigationProgress](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application.navigationprogress#system-windows-application-navigationprogress)
  * [Application.Navigated](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application.navigated#system-windows-application-navigated)
  * [Application.NavigationFailed](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application.navigationfailed#system-windows-application-navigationfailed)
  * [Application.NavigationStopped](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application.navigationstopped#system-windows-application-navigationstopped)
  * [Application.LoadCompleted](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application.loadcompleted#system-windows-application-loadcompleted)
  * [Application.FragmentNavigation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application.fragmentnavigation#system-windows-application-fragmentnavigation)


Every time [NavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice) raises an event, the [Application](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application) class raises the corresponding event. [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame) and [NavigationWindow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow) offer the same events to detect navigation within their respective scopes.
In some cases, a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) might be interested in these events. For example, a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) might handle the [NavigationService.Navigating](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.navigating#system-windows-navigation-navigationservice-navigating) event to determine whether or not to cancel navigation away from itself. This is shown in the following example.
XAML Copy
```
<Page
    xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
    xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
    x:Class="SDKSample.CancelNavigationPage">
  <Button Click="button_Click">Navigate to Another Page</Button>
</Page>

```

C# Copy
```
using System;
using System.Windows;
using System.Windows.Controls;
using System.Windows.Navigation;

namespace SDKSample
{
    public partial class CancelNavigationPage : Page
    {
        public CancelNavigationPage(
        {
            InitializeComponent();

            // Can only access the NavigationService when the page has been loaded
            this.Loaded += new RoutedEventHandler(CancelNavigationPage_Loaded);
            this.Unloaded += new RoutedEventHandler(CancelNavigationPage_Unloaded);
        }

        void button_Click(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
        {
            // Force WPF to download this page again
            this.NavigationService.Navigate(new Uri("AnotherPage.xaml", UriKind.Relative));
        }

        void CancelNavigationPage_Loaded(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
        {
            this.NavigationService.Navigating += new NavigatingCancelEventHandler(NavigationService_Navigating);
        }

        void CancelNavigationPage_Unloaded(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
        {
            this.NavigationService.Navigating -= new NavigatingCancelEventHandler(NavigationService_Navigating);
        }

        void NavigationService_Navigating(object sender, NavigatingCancelEventArgs e)
        {
            // Does the user really want to navigate to another page?
            MessageBoxResult result;
            result = MessageBox.Show("Do you want to leave this page?", "Navigation Request", MessageBoxButton.YesNo);

            // If the user doesn't want to navigate away, cancel the navigation
            if (result == MessageBoxResult.No) e.Cancel = true;
        }
    }
}

```
```

Namespace SDKSample
    Partial Public Class CancelNavigationPage
        Inherits Page
        Public Sub New()
            InitializeComponent()

            ' Can only access the NavigationService when the page has been loaded
            AddHandler Loaded, AddressOf CancelNavigationPage_Loaded
            AddHandler Unloaded, AddressOf CancelNavigationPage_Unloaded
        End Sub

        Private Sub button_Click(ByVal sender As Object, ByVal e As RoutedEventArgs)
            ' Force WPF to download this page again
            Me.NavigationService.Navigate(New Uri("AnotherPage.xaml", UriKind.Relative))
        End Sub

        Private Sub CancelNavigationPage_Loaded(ByVal sender As Object, ByVal e As RoutedEventArgs)
            AddHandler NavigationService.Navigating, AddressOf NavigationService_Navigating
        End Sub

        Private Sub CancelNavigationPage_Unloaded(ByVal sender As Object, ByVal e As RoutedEventArgs)
            RemoveHandler NavigationService.Navigating, AddressOf NavigationService_Navigating
        End Sub

        Private Sub NavigationService_Navigating(ByVal sender As Object, ByVal e As NavigatingCancelEventArgs)
            ' Does the user really want to navigate to another page?
            Dim result As MessageBoxResult
            result = MessageBox.Show("Do you want to leave this page?", "Navigation Request", MessageBoxButton.YesNo)

            ' If the user doesn't want to navigate away, cancel the navigation
            If result = MessageBoxResult.No Then
                e.Cancel = True
            End If
        End Sub
    End Class
End Namespace

```

If you register a handler with a navigation event from a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page), as the preceding example does, you must also unregister the event handler. If you don't, there may be side effects with respect to how WPF navigation remembers [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) navigation using the journal.
### Remembering Navigation with the Journal
WPF uses two stacks to remember the pages that you have navigated from: a back stack and a forward stack. When you navigate from the current [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) to a new [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) or forward to an existing [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page), the current [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) is added to the _back stack_. When you navigate from the current [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) back to the previous [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page), the current [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) is added to the _forward stack_. The back stack, the forward stack, and the functionality to manage them, are collectively referred to as the journal. Each item in the back stack and the forward stack is an instance of the [JournalEntry](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.journalentry) class, and is referred to as a _journal entry_.
#### Navigating the Journal from Internet Explorer
Conceptually, the journal operates the same way that the **Back** and **Forward** buttons in Internet Explorer do. These are shown in the following figure.
For XBAPs that are hosted by Internet Explorer, WPF integrates the journal into the navigation UI of Internet Explorer. This allows users to navigate pages in an XBAP by using the **Back** , **Forward** , and **Recent Pages** buttons in Internet Explorer.
In Internet Explorer, when a user navigates away from and back to an XBAP, only the journal entries for pages that were not kept alive are retained in the journal. For discussion on keeping pages alive, see [Page Lifetime and the Journal](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/navigation-overview#PageLifetime) later in this topic.
By default, the text for each [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) that appears in the **Recent Pages** list of Internet Explorer is the URI for the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page). In many cases, this is not particularly meaningful to the user. Fortunately, you can change the text using one the following options:
  1. The attached `JournalEntry.Name` attribute value.
  2. The `Page.Title` attribute value.
  3. The `Page.WindowTitle` attribute value and the URI for the current [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page).
  4. The URI for the current [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page). (Default)


The order in which the options are listed matches the order of precedence for finding the text. For example, if `JournalEntry.Name` is set, the other values are ignored.
The following example uses the `Page.Title` attribute to change the text that appears for a journal entry.

<Page

    xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
    x:Class="SDKSample.PageWithTitle"
    Title="This is the title of the journal entry for this page.">

```

#### Navigating the Journal Using WPF
Although a user can navigate the journal by using the **Back** , **Forward** , and **Recent Pages** in Internet Explorer, you can also navigate the journal using both declarative and programmatic mechanisms provided by WPF. One reason to do this is to provide custom navigation UIs in your pages.
You can declaratively add journal navigation support by using the navigation commands exposed by [NavigationCommands](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.input.navigationcommands). The following example demonstrates how to use the `BrowseBack` navigation command.
XAML Copy
```
<Page
    xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
