### Navigation Lifetime
There are many ways to initiate navigation, as you've seen. When navigation is initiated, and while navigation is in progress, you can track and influence the navigation using the following events that are implemented by [NavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice):
  * [Navigating](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.navigating#system-windows-navigation-navigationservice-navigating). Occurs when a new navigation is requested. Can be used to cancel the navigation.
  * [NavigationProgress](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.navigationprogress#system-windows-navigation-navigationservice-navigationprogress). Occurs periodically during a download to provide navigation progress information.
  * [Navigated](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.navigated#system-windows-navigation-navigationservice-navigated). Occurs when the page has been located and downloaded.
  * [NavigationStopped](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.navigationstopped#system-windows-navigation-navigationservice-navigationstopped). Occurs when the navigation is stopped (by calling [StopLoading](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.stoploading)), or when a new navigation is requested while a current navigation is in progress.
  * [NavigationFailed](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.navigationfailed#system-windows-navigation-navigationservice-navigationfailed). Occurs when an error is raised while navigating to the requested content.
  * [LoadCompleted](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.loadcompleted#system-windows-navigation-navigationservice-loadcompleted). Occurs when content that was navigated to is loaded and parsed, and has begun rendering.
  * [FragmentNavigation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.fragmentnavigation#system-windows-navigation-navigationservice-fragmentnavigation). Occurs when navigation to a content fragment begins, which happens:
    * Immediately, if the desired fragment is in the current content.
    * After the source content has been loaded, if the desired fragment is in different content.


The navigation events are raised in the order that is illustrated by the following figure.
In general, a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) isn't concerned about these events. It is more likely that an application is concerned with them and, for that reason, these events are also raised by the [Application](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application) class:
  * [Application.Navigating](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application.navigating#system-windows-application-navigating)
  * [Application.NavigationProgress](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application.navigationprogress#system-windows-application-navigationprogress)
  * [Application.Navigated](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application.navigated#system-windows-application-navigated)
  * [Application.NavigationFailed](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application.navigationfailed#system-windows-application-navigationfailed)
  * [Application.NavigationStopped](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application.navigationstopped#system-windows-application-navigationstopped)
  * [Application.LoadCompleted](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application.loadcompleted#system-windows-application-loadcompleted)
  * [Application.FragmentNavigation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application.fragmentnavigation#system-windows-application-fragmentnavigation)


Every time [NavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice) raises an event, the [Application](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application) class raises the corresponding event. [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame) and [NavigationWindow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow) offer the same events to detect navigation within their respective scopes.
In some cases, a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) might be interested in these events. For example, a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) might handle the [NavigationService.Navigating](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.navigating#system-windows-navigation-navigationservice-navigating) event to determine whether or not to cancel navigation away from itself. This is shown in the following example.
XAML Copy
```
<Page
    xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
    xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
    x:Class="SDKSample.CancelNavigationPage">
  <Button Click="button_Click">Navigate to Another Page</Button>
</Page>

```

C# Copy
```
using System;
using System.Windows;
using System.Windows.Controls;
using System.Windows.Navigation;

namespace SDKSample
{
    public partial class CancelNavigationPage : Page
    {
        public CancelNavigationPage(
        {
            InitializeComponent();

            // Can only access the NavigationService when the page has been loaded
            this.Loaded += new RoutedEventHandler(CancelNavigationPage_Loaded);
            this.Unloaded += new RoutedEventHandler(CancelNavigationPage_Unloaded);
        }

        void button_Click(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
        {
            // Force WPF to download this page again
            this.NavigationService.Navigate(new Uri("AnotherPage.xaml", UriKind.Relative));
        }

        void CancelNavigationPage_Loaded(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
        {
            this.NavigationService.Navigating += new NavigatingCancelEventHandler(NavigationService_Navigating);
        }

        void CancelNavigationPage_Unloaded(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
        {
            this.NavigationService.Navigating -= new NavigatingCancelEventHandler(NavigationService_Navigating);
        }

        void NavigationService_Navigating(object sender, NavigatingCancelEventArgs e)
        {
            // Does the user really want to navigate to another page?
            MessageBoxResult result;
            result = MessageBox.Show("Do you want to leave this page?", "Navigation Request", MessageBoxButton.YesNo);

            // If the user doesn't want to navigate away, cancel the navigation
            if (result == MessageBoxResult.No) e.Cancel = true;
        }
    }
}

            AddHandler Loaded, AddressOf CancelNavigationPage_Loaded
            AddHandler Unloaded, AddressOf CancelNavigationPage_Unloaded

            Dim result As MessageBoxResult
            result = MessageBox.Show("Do you want to leave this page?", "Navigation Request", MessageBoxButton.YesNo)

            ' If the user doesn't want to navigate away, cancel the navigation
            If result = MessageBoxResult.No Then
                e.Cancel = True
            End If
        End Sub

If you register a handler with a navigation event from a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page), as the preceding example does, you must also unregister the event handler. If you don't, there may be side effects with respect to how WPF navigation remembers [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) navigation using the journal.
### Remembering Navigation with the Journal
WPF uses two stacks to remember the pages that you have navigated from: a back stack and a forward stack. When you navigate from the current [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) to a new [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) or forward to an existing [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page), the current [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) is added to the _back stack_. When you navigate from the current [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) back to the previous [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page), the current [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) is added to the _forward stack_. The back stack, the forward stack, and the functionality to manage them, are collectively referred to as the journal. Each item in the back stack and the forward stack is an instance of the [JournalEntry](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.journalentry) class, and is referred to as a _journal entry_.
#### Navigating the Journal from Internet Explorer
Conceptually, the journal operates the same way that the **Back** and **Forward** buttons in Internet Explorer do. These are shown in the following figure.
For XBAPs that are hosted by Internet Explorer, WPF integrates the journal into the navigation UI of Internet Explorer. This allows users to navigate pages in an XBAP by using the **Back** , **Forward** , and **Recent Pages** buttons in Internet Explorer.
In Internet Explorer, when a user navigates away from and back to an XBAP, only the journal entries for pages that were not kept alive are retained in the journal. For discussion on keeping pages alive, see [Page Lifetime and the Journal](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/navigation-overview#PageLifetime) later in this topic.
By default, the text for each [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) that appears in the **Recent Pages** list of Internet Explorer is the URI for the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page). In many cases, this is not particularly meaningful to the user. Fortunately, you can change the text using one the following options:
  1. The attached `JournalEntry.Name` attribute value.
  2. The `Page.Title` attribute value.
  3. The `Page.WindowTitle` attribute value and the URI for the current [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page).
  4. The URI for the current [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page). (Default)


The order in which the options are listed matches the order of precedence for finding the text. For example, if `JournalEntry.Name` is set, the other values are ignored.
The following example uses the `Page.Title` attribute to change the text that appears for a journal entry.

#### Navigating the Journal Using WPF
Although a user can navigate the journal by using the **Back** , **Forward** , and **Recent Pages** in Internet Explorer, you can also navigate the journal using both declarative and programmatic mechanisms provided by WPF. One reason to do this is to provide custom navigation UIs in your pages.
You can declaratively add journal navigation support by using the navigation commands exposed by [NavigationCommands](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.input.navigationcommands). The following example demonstrates how to use the `BrowseBack` navigation command.
XAML Copy
```
<Page
    xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
    xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
    x:Class="SDKSample.NavigationCommandsPage">

```

XAML Copy
```
<Hyperlink Command="NavigationCommands.BrowseBack">Back</Hyperlink>

```

XAML Copy
```
<Hyperlink Command="NavigationCommands.BrowseForward">Forward</Hyperlink>

```

XAML Copy
```
</Page>

```

You can programmatically navigate the journal by using one of the following members of the [NavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice) class:
  * [GoBack](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.goback)
  * [GoForward](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.goforward)
  * [CanGoBack](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.cangoback)
  * [CanGoForward](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.cangoforward)


The journal can also be manipulated programmatically, as discussed in [Retaining Content State with Navigation History](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/navigation-overview#RetainingContentStateWithNavigationHistory) later in this topic.
### Page Lifetime and the Journal
Consider an XBAP with several pages that contain rich content, including graphics, animations, and media. The memory footprint for pages like these could be quite large, particularly if video and audio media are used. Given that the journal "remembers" pages that have been navigated to, such an XBAP could quickly consume a large and noticeable amount of memory.
For this reason, the default behavior of the journal is to store [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) metadata in each journal entry rather than a reference to a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) object. When a journal entry is navigated to, its [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) metadata is used to create a new instance of the specified [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page). As a consequence, each [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) that is navigated has the lifetime that is illustrated by the following figure.
Although using the default journaling behavior can save on memory consumption, per-page rendering performance might be reduced; reinstantiating a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) can be time-intensive, particularly if it has a lot of content. If you need to retain a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) instance in the journal, you can draw on two techniques for doing so. First, you can programmatically navigate to a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) object by calling the [NavigationService.Navigate](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.navigate) method.
Second, you can specify that WPF retain an instance of a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) in the journal by setting the [KeepAlive](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page.keepalive) property to `true` (the default is `false`). As shown in the following example, you can set [KeepAlive](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page.keepalive) declaratively in markup.
XAML Copy
```
<Page
    xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
    xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
    x:Class="SDKSample.KeepAlivePage"
    KeepAlive="True">
  
  An instance of this page is stored in the journal.
  
</Page>

```

The lifetime of a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) that is kept alive is subtly different from one that is not. The first time a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) that is kept alive is navigated to, it is instantiated just like a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) that is not kept alive. However, because an instance of the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) is retained in the journal, it is never instantiated again for as long as it remains in the journal. Consequently, if a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) has initialization logic that needs to be called every time the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) is navigated to, you should move it from the constructor into a handler for the [Loaded](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.frameworkelement.loaded#system-windows-frameworkelement-loaded) event. As shown in the following figure, the [Loaded](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.frameworkelement.loaded#system-windows-frameworkelement-loaded) and [Unloaded](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.frameworkelement.unloaded#system-windows-frameworkelement-unloaded) events are still raised each time a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) is navigated to and from, respectively.
When a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) is not kept alive, you should not do either of the following:
  * Store a reference to it, or any part of it.
  * Register event handlers with events that are not implemented by it.


Doing either of these will create references that force the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) to be retained in memory, even after it has been removed from the journal.
In general, you should prefer the default [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) behavior of not keeping a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) alive. However, this has state implications that are discussed in the next section.
### Retaining Content State with Navigation History
If a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) is not kept alive, and it has controls that collect data from the user, what happens to the data if a user navigates away from and back to the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page)? From a user experience perspective, the user should expect to see the data they entered previously. Unfortunately, because a new instance of the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) is created with each navigation, the controls that collected the data are reinstantiated and the data is lost.
Fortunately, the journal provides support for remembering data across [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) navigations, including control data. Specifically, the journal entry for each [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) acts as a temporary container for the associated [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) state. The following steps outline how this support is used when a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) is navigated from:
  1. An entry for the current [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) is added to the journal.
  2. The state of the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) is stored with the journal entry for that page, which is added to the back stack.
  3. The new [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) is navigated to.


When the page [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) is navigated back to, using the journal, the following steps take place:
  1. The [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) (the top journal entry on the back stack) is instantiated.
  2. The [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) is refreshed with the state that was stored with the journal entry for the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page).
  3. The [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) is navigated back to.


WPF automatically uses this support when the following controls are used on a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page):
  * [CheckBox](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.checkbox)
  * [ComboBox](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.combobox)
  * [Expander](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.expander)
  * [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame)
  * [ListBox](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.listbox)
  * [ListBoxItem](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.listboxitem)
  * [MenuItem](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.menuitem)
  * [ProgressBar](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.progressbar)
  * [RadioButton](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.radiobutton)
  * [Slider](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.slider)
  * [TabControl](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.tabcontrol)
  * [TabItem](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.tabitem)
  * [TextBox](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.textbox)


If a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) uses these controls, data entered into them is remembered across [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) navigations, as demonstrated by the **Favorite Color**[ListBox](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.listbox) in the following figure.
When a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) has controls other than those in the preceding list, or when state is stored in custom objects, you need to write code to cause the journal to remember state across [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) navigations.
If you need to remember small pieces of state across [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) navigations, you can use dependency properties (see [DependencyProperty](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.dependencyproperty)) that are configured with the [FrameworkPropertyMetadata.Journal](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.frameworkpropertymetadata.journal) metadata flag.
If the state that your [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) needs to remember across navigations comprises multiple pieces of data, you may find it less code intensive to encapsulate your state in a single class and implement the [IProvideCustomContentState](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.iprovidecustomcontentstate) interface.
If you need to navigate through various states of a single [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page), without navigating from the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) itself, you can use [IProvideCustomContentState](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.iprovidecustomcontentstate) and [NavigationService.AddBackEntry](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice.addbackentry).
### Cookies
Another way that WPF applications can store data is with cookies, which are created, updated, and deleted by using the [SetCookie](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application.setcookie) and [GetCookie](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application.getcookie) methods. The cookies that you can create in WPF are the same cookies that other types of Web applications use; cookies are arbitrary pieces of data that are stored by an application on a client machine either during or across application sessions. Cookie data typically takes the form of a name/value pair in the following format.
_Name_ `=` _Value_
When the data is passed to [SetCookie](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application.setcookie), along with the [Uri](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.uri) of the location for which the cookie should be set, a cookie is created in-memory, and it is only available for the duration of the current application session. This type of cookie is referred to as a _session cookie_.
To store a cookie across application sessions, an expiration date must be added to the cookie, using the following format.
_NAME_ `=` _VALUE_ `; expires=DAY, DD-MMM-YYYY HH:MM:SS GMT`
A cookie with an expiration date is stored in the current Windows installation's Temporary Internet Files folder until the cookie expires. Such a cookie is known as a _persistent cookie_ because it persists across application sessions.
You retrieve both session and persistent cookies by calling the [GetCookie](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application.getcookie) method, passing the [Uri](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.uri) of the location where the cookie was set with the [SetCookie](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application.setcookie) method.
The following are some of the ways that cookies are supported in WPF:
  * WPF standalone applications and XBAPs can both create and manage cookies.
  * Cookies that are created by an XBAP can be accessed from the browser.
  * XBAPs from the same domain can create and share cookies.
  * XBAPs and HTML pages from the same domain can create and share cookies.
  * Cookies are dispatched when XBAPs and loose XAML pages make Web requests.
  * Both top-level XBAPs and XBAPs hosted in IFRAMES can access cookies.
  * Cookie support in WPF is the same for all supported browsers.
  * In Internet Explorer, P3P policy that pertains to cookies is honored by WPF, particularly with respect to first-party and third-party XBAPs.


### Structured Navigation
If you need to pass data from one [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) to another, you can pass the data as arguments to a non-parameterless constructor of the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page). Note that if you use this technique, you must keep the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) alive; if not, the next time you navigate to the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page), WPF reinstantiates the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) by using the parameterless constructor.
Alternatively, your [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) can implement properties that are set with the data that needs to be passed. Things become tricky, however, when a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) needs to pass data back to the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) that navigated to it. The problem is that navigation doesn't natively support mechanisms for guaranteeing that a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) will be returned to after it is navigated from. Essentially, navigation doesn't support call/return semantics. To solve this problem, WPF provides the [PageFunction<T>](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.pagefunction-1) class that you can use to ensure that a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) is returned to in a predictable and structured fashion. For more information, see [Structured Navigation Overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/structured-navigation-overview).
## The NavigationWindow Class
To this point, you've seen the gamut of navigation services that you are most likely to use to build applications with navigable content. These services were discussed in the context of XBAPs, although they are not limited to XBAPs. Modern operating systems and Windows applications take advantage of the browser experience of modern users to incorporate browser-style navigation into standalone applications. Common examples include:
  * **Word Thesaurus** : Navigate word choices.
  * **File Explorer** : Navigate files and folders.
  * **Wizards** : Breaking down a complex task into multiple pages that can be navigated between. An example is the Windows Components Wizard that handles adding and removing Windows features.


To incorporate browser-style navigation into your standalone applications, you can use the [NavigationWindow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow) class. [NavigationWindow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow) derives from [Window](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.window) and extends it with the same support for navigation that XBAPs provide. You can use [NavigationWindow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow) as either the main window of your standalone application or as a secondary window such as a dialog box.
To implement a [NavigationWindow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow), as with most top-level classes in WPF ([Window](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.window), [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page), and so on), you use a combination of markup and code-behind. This is shown in the following example.
XAML Copy
```
<NavigationWindow
    xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
    xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
    x:Class="SDKSample.MainWindow" 
    Source="HomePage.xaml"/>

```

C# Copy
```
using System.Windows.Navigation;

namespace SDKSample
{
    public partial class MainWindow : NavigationWindow
    {
        public MainWindow(
        {
            InitializeComponent();
        }
    }
}

```
```

Namespace SDKSample
    Partial Public Class MainWindow
        Inherits NavigationWindow
        Public Sub New()
            InitializeComponent()
        End Sub
    End Class
End Namespace

```

This code creates a [NavigationWindow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow) that automatically navigates to a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) (HomePage.xaml) when the [NavigationWindow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow) is opened. If the [NavigationWindow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow) is the main application window, you can use the `StartupUri` attribute to launch it. This is shown in the following markup.
XAML Copy
```
<Application
    xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
    StartupUri="MainWindow.xaml" />

```

The following figure shows the [NavigationWindow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow) as the main window of a standalone application.
From the figure, you can see that the [NavigationWindow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow) has a title, even though it wasn't set in the [NavigationWindow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow) implementation code from the preceding example. Instead, the title is set using the [WindowTitle](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page.windowtitle) property, which is shown in the following code.
XAML Copy
```
<Page 
    xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
    Title="Home Page"
    WindowTitle="NavigationWindow">

```

XAML Copy
```
</Page>

```

Setting the [WindowWidth](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page.windowwidth) and [WindowHeight](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page.windowheight) properties also affects the [NavigationWindow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow).
Usually, you implement your own [NavigationWindow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow) when you need to customize either its behavior or its appearance. If you do neither, you can use a shortcut. If you specify the pack URI of a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) as the [StartupUri](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application.startupuri) in a standalone application, [Application](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.application) automatically creates a [NavigationWindow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow) to host the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page). The following markup shows how to enable this.
XAML Copy
```
<Application
    xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
    StartupUri="HomePage.xaml" />

```

If you want a secondary application window such as a dialog box to be a [NavigationWindow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow), you can use the code in the following example to open it.
C# Copy
```
// Open a navigation window as a dialog box
NavigationWindowDialogBox dlg = new NavigationWindowDialogBox();
dlg.Source = new Uri("HomePage.xaml", UriKind.Relative);
dlg.Owner = this;
dlg.ShowDialog();

```
```
' Open a navigation window as a dialog box
Dim dlg As New NavigationWindowDialogBox()
dlg.Source = New Uri("HomePage.xaml", UriKind.Relative)
dlg.Owner = Me
dlg.ShowDialog()

```

The following figure shows the result.
As you can see, [NavigationWindow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow) displays Internet Explorer-style **Back** and **Forward** buttons that allow users to navigate the journal. These buttons provide the same user experience, as shown in the following figure.
If your pages provide their own journal navigation support and UI, you can hide the **Back** and **Forward** buttons displayed by [NavigationWindow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow) by setting the value of the [ShowsNavigationUI](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow.showsnavigationui) property to `false`.
Alternatively, you can use customization support in WPF to replace the UI of the [NavigationWindow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow) itself.
## The Frame Class
Both the browser and [NavigationWindow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow) are windows that host navigable content. In some cases, applications have content that does not need to be hosted by an entire window. Instead, such content be hosted inside other content. You can insert navigable content into other content by using the [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame) class. [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame) provides the same support as [NavigationWindow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow) and XBAPs.
The following example shows how to add a [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame) to a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) declaratively by using the `Frame` element.
XAML Copy
```
<Page 
  xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
  WindowTitle="Page that Hosts a Frame"
  WindowWidth="250"
  WindowHeight="250">

```

XAML Copy
```
<Frame Source="FramePage1.xaml" />

```

XAML Copy
```
</Page>

```

This markup sets the `Source` attribute of the `Frame` element with a pack URI for the [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) that the [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame) should initially navigate to. The following figure shows an XBAP with a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) that has a [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame) that has navigated between several pages.
You don't only have to use [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame) inside the content of a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page). It is also common to host a [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame) inside the content of a [Window](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.window).
By default, [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame) only uses its own journal in the absence of another journal. If a [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame) is part of content that is hosted inside either a [NavigationWindow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow) or an XBAP, [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame) uses the journal that belongs to the [NavigationWindow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow) or XBAP. Sometimes, though, a [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame) might need to be responsible for its own journal. One reason to do so is to allow journal navigation within the pages that are hosted by a [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame). This is illustrated by the following figure.
In this case, you can configure the [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame) to use its own journal by setting the [JournalOwnership](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame.journalownership) property of the [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame) to [OwnsJournal](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.journalownership#system-windows-navigation-journalownership-ownsjournal). This is shown in the following markup.
XAML Copy
```
<Page 
  xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
  WindowTitle="Page that Hosts a Frame"
  WindowWidth="250"
  WindowHeight="250">

```

XAML Copy
```
<Frame Source="FramePage1.xaml" JournalOwnership="OwnsJournal" />

```

XAML Copy
```
</Page>

```

The following figure illustrates the effect of navigating within a [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame) that uses its own journal.
Notice that the journal entries are shown by the navigation UI in the [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame), rather than by Internet Explorer.
If a [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame) is part of content that is hosted in a [Window](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.window), [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame) uses its own journal and, consequently, displays its own navigation UI.
If your user experience requires a [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame) to provide its own journal without showing the navigation UI, you can hide the navigation UI by setting the [NavigationUIVisibility](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame.navigationuivisibility) to [Hidden](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.visibility#system-windows-visibility-hidden). This is shown in the following markup.
XAML Copy
```
<Page 
  xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
  WindowTitle="Page that Hosts a Frame"
  WindowWidth="250"
  WindowHeight="250">

```

XAML Copy
```
<Frame 
  Source="FramePage1.xaml" 
  JournalOwnership="OwnsJournal" 
  NavigationUIVisibility="Hidden" />

```

XAML Copy
```
</Page>

```

## Navigation Hosts
[Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame) and [NavigationWindow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow) are classes that are known as navigation hosts. A _navigation host_ is a class that can navigate to and display content. To accomplish this, each navigation host uses its own [NavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice) and journal. The basic construction of a navigation host is shown in the following figure.
Essentially, this allows [NavigationWindow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow) and [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame) to provide the same navigation support that an XBAP provides when hosted in the browser.
Besides using [NavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice) and a journal, navigation hosts implement the same members that [NavigationService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationservice) implements. This is illustrated by the following figure.
This allows you to program navigation support directly against them. You may consider this if you need to provide a custom navigation UI for a [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame) that is hosted in a [Window](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.window). Furthermore, both types implement additional, navigation-related members, including `BackStack` ([NavigationWindow.BackStack](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow.backstack), [Frame.BackStack](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame.backstack)) and `ForwardStack` ([NavigationWindow.ForwardStack](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow.forwardstack), [Frame.ForwardStack](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame.forwardstack)), which allow you to enumerate the journal entries in the back stack and forward stack, respectively.
As mentioned earlier, more than one journal can exist within an application. The following figure provides an example of when this can happen.
## Navigating to Content Other than XAML Pages
Throughout this topic, [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) and pack XBAPs have been used to demonstrate the various navigation capabilities of WPF. However, a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) that is compiled into an application is not the only type of content that can be navigated to, and pack XBAPs aren't the only way to identify content.
As this section demonstrates, you can also navigate to loose XAML files, HTML files, and objects.
### Navigating to Loose XAML Files
A loose XAML file is a file with the following characteristics:
  * Contains only XAML (that is, no code).
  * Has an appropriate namespace declaration.
  * Has the .xaml file name extension.


For example, consider the following content that is stored as a loose XAML file, Person.xaml.
XAML Copy
```
<!-- Person.xaml -->
<TextBlock xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation">
  <TextBlock FontWeight="Bold">Name:</TextBlock>
  <TextBlock>Nancy Davolio</TextBlock>
  <LineBreak />
  <TextBlock FontWeight="Bold">Favorite Color:</TextBlock>
  <TextBlock>Yellow</TextBlock>
</TextBlock>

```

When you double-click the file, the browser opens and navigates to and displays the content. This is shown in the following figure.
You can display a loose XAML file from the following:
  * A Web site on the local machine, the intranet, or the Internet.
  * A Universal Naming Convention (UNC) file share.
  * The local disk.


A loose XAML file can be added to the browser's favorites, or be the browser's home page.
For more information about publishing and launching loose XAML pages, see [Deploying a WPF Application](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/app-development/deploying-a-wpf-application-wpf).
One limitation with respect to loose XAML is that you can only host content that is safe to run in partial trust. For example, `Window` cannot be the root element of a loose XAML file. For more information, see [WPF Partial Trust Security](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/wpf-partial-trust-security).
### Navigating to HTML Files by Using Frame
As you might expect, you can also navigate to HTML. You simply need to provide a URI that uses the http scheme. For example, the following XAML shows a [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame) that navigates to an HTML page.
XAML Copy
```
<Frame Source="http://www.microsoft.com/default.aspx" />

```

Navigating to HTML requires special permissions. For example, you can't navigate from an XBAP that is running in the Internet zone partial trust security sandbox. For more information, see [WPF Partial Trust Security](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/wpf-partial-trust-security).
### Navigating to HTML Files by Using the WebBrowser Control
The [WebBrowser](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.webbrowser) control supports HTML document hosting, navigation and script/managed code interoperability. For detailed information regarding the [WebBrowser](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.webbrowser) control, see [WebBrowser](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.webbrowser).
Like [Frame](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.frame), navigating to HTML using [WebBrowser](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.webbrowser) requires special permissions. For example, from a partial-trust application, you can navigate only to HTML located at the site of origin. For more information, see [WPF Partial Trust Security](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/wpf-partial-trust-security).
### Navigating to Custom Objects
If you have data that is stored as custom objects, one way to display that data is to create a [Page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.page) with content that is bound to those objects (see [Data Binding Overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/data/)). If you don't need the overhead of creating an entire page just to display the objects, you can navigate directly to them instead.
Consider the `Person` class that is implemented in the following code.
C# Copy
```
using System.Windows.Media;

namespace SDKSample
{
    public class Person
    {
        string name;
        Color favoriteColor;

        public Person( { }
        public Person(string name, Color favoriteColor)
        {
            this.name = name;
            this.favoriteColor = favoriteColor;
        }

        public string Name
        {
            get { return this.name; }
            set { this.name = value; }
        }

        public Color FavoriteColor
        {
            get { return this.favoriteColor; }
            set { this.favoriteColor = value; }
        }
    }
}

```
```

Namespace SDKSample
    Public Class Person
        Private _name As String
        Private _favoriteColor As Color

        Public Sub New()
        End Sub
        Public Sub New(ByVal name As String, ByVal favoriteColor As Color)
            Me._name = name
            Me._favoriteColor = favoriteColor
        End Sub

        Public Property Name() As String
            Get
                Return Me._name
            End Get
            Set(ByVal value As String)
                Me._name = value
            End Set
        End Property

        Public Property FavoriteColor() As Color
            Get
                Return Me._favoriteColor
            End Get
            Set(ByVal value As Color)
                Me._favoriteColor = value
            End Set
        End Property
    End Class
End Namespace

```

To navigate to it, you call the [NavigationWindow.Navigate](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.navigation.navigationwindow.navigate) method, as demonstrated by the following code.
XAML Copy
```
<Page 
  xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
  xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
  x:Class="SDKSample.HomePage"
  WindowTitle="Page that Navigates to an Object">

```

XAML Copy
```
<Hyperlink Name="hyperlink" Click="hyperlink_Click">
  Navigate to Nancy Davolio
</Hyperlink>

```

XAML Copy
```
</Page>

```

C# Copy
```
using System.Windows;
using System.Windows.Controls;
using System.Windows.Media;

namespace SDKSample
{
    public partial class HomePage : Page
    {
        public HomePage(
        {
            InitializeComponent();
        }

        void hyperlink_Click(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
        {
            Person person = new Person("Nancy Davolio", Colors.Yellow);
            this.NavigationService.Navigate(person);
        }
    }
}

```
```

Namespace SDKSample
    Partial Public Class HomePage
        Inherits Page
        Public Sub New()
            InitializeComponent()
        End Sub

        Private Sub hyperlink_Click(ByVal sender As Object, ByVal e As RoutedEventArgs)
            Dim person As New Person("Nancy Davolio", Colors.Yellow)
            Me.NavigationService.Navigate(person)
        End Sub
    End Class
End Namespace

```

The following figure shows the result.
From this figure, you can see that nothing useful is displayed. In fact, the value that is displayed is the return value of the `ToString` method for the **Person** object; by default, this is the only value that WPF can use to represent your object. You could override the `ToString` method to return more meaningful information, although it will still only be a string value. One technique you can use that takes advantage of the presentation capabilities of WPF is to use a data template. You can implement a data template that WPF can associate with an object of a particular type. The following code shows a data template for the `Person` object.
XAML Copy
```
<Application
    xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
    xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
    xmlns:local="clr-namespace:SDKSample" 
    x:Class="SDKSample.App"
    StartupUri="HomePage.xaml">

  <Application.Resources>

    <!-- Data Template for the Person Class -->
    <DataTemplate DataType="{x:Type local:Person}">
      <TextBlock xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation">
        <TextBlock FontWeight="Bold">Name:</TextBlock>
        <TextBlock Text="{Binding Path=Name}" />
        <LineBreak />
        <TextBlock FontWeight="Bold">Favorite Color:</TextBlock>
        <TextBlock Text="{Binding Path=FavoriteColor}" />
      </TextBlock>
    </DataTemplate>
    
  </Application.Resources>

</Application>

```

Here, the data template is associated with the `Person` type by using the `x:Type` markup extension in the `DataType` attribute. The data template then binds `TextBlock` elements (see [TextBlock](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.textblock)) to the properties of the `Person` class. The following figure shows the updated appearance of the `Person` object.
An advantage of this technique is the consistency you gain by being able to reuse the data template to display your objects consistently anywhere in your application.
For more information on data templates, see [Data Templating Overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/data/data-templating-overview).
## Security
WPF navigation support allows XBAPs to be navigated to across the Internet, and it allows applications to host third-party content. To protect both applications and users from harmful behavior, WPF provides a variety of security features that are discussed in [Security](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/security-wpf) and [WPF Partial Trust Security](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/wpf-partial-trust-security).

# Panels Overview

Feedback
[Panel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.panel) elements are components that control the rendering of elements—their size and dimensions, their position, and the arrangement of their child content. The Windows Presentation Foundation (WPF) provides a number of predefined [Panel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.panel) elements as well as the ability to construct custom [Panel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.panel) elements.

## The Panel Class
[Panel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.panel) is the base class for all elements that provide layout support in Windows Presentation Foundation (WPF). Derived [Panel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.panel) elements are used to position and arrange elements in Extensible Application Markup Language (XAML) and code.
The WPF includes a comprehensive suite of derived panel implementations that enable many complex layouts. These derived classes expose properties and methods that enable most standard user interface (UI) scenarios. Developers who are unable to find a child arrangement behavior that meets their needs can create new layouts by overriding the [ArrangeOverride](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.frameworkelement.arrangeoverride) and [MeasureOverride](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.frameworkelement.measureoverride) methods. For more information on custom layout behaviors, see [Custom Panel Elements](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/controls/panels-overview#Panels_custom_panel_elements).
## Panel Common Members
All [Panel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.panel) elements support the base sizing and positioning properties defined by [FrameworkElement](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.frameworkelement), including [Height](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.frameworkelement.height), [Width](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.frameworkelement.width), [HorizontalAlignment](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.frameworkelement.horizontalalignment), [VerticalAlignment](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.frameworkelement.verticalalignment), [Margin](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.frameworkelement.margin), and [LayoutTransform](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.frameworkelement.layouttransform). For additional information on positioning properties defined by [FrameworkElement](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.frameworkelement), see [Alignment, Margins, and Padding Overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/advanced/alignment-margins-and-padding-overview).
[Panel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.panel) exposes additional properties that are of critical importance in understanding and using layout. The [Background](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.panel.background) property is used to fill the area between the boundaries of a derived panel element with a [Brush](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.media.brush). [Children](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.panel.children) represents the child collection of elements that the [Panel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.panel) is comprised of. [InternalChildren](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.panel.internalchildren) represents the content of the [Children](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.panel.children) collection plus those members generated by data binding. Both consist of a [UIElementCollection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.uielementcollection) of child elements hosted within the parent [Panel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.panel).
Panel also exposes a [Panel.ZIndex](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.panel.zindex) attached property that can be used to achieve layered order in a derived [Panel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.panel). Members of a panel's [Children](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.panel.children) collection with a higher [Panel.ZIndex](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.panel.zindex) value appear in front of those with a lower [Panel.ZIndex](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.panel.zindex) value. This is particularly useful for panels such as [Canvas](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.canvas) and [Grid](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.grid) which allow children to share the same coordinate space.
[Panel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.panel) also defines the [OnRender](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.panel.onrender) method, which can be used to override the default presentation behavior of a [Panel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.panel).
#### Attached Properties
Derived panel elements make extensive use of attached properties. An attached property is a specialized form of dependency property that does not have the conventional common language runtime (CLR) property "wrapper". Attached properties have a specialized syntax in Extensible Application Markup Language (XAML), which can be seen in several of the examples that follow.
One purpose of an attached property is to allow child elements to store unique values of a property that is actually defined by a parent element. An application of this functionality is having child elements inform the parent how they wish to be presented in the user interface (UI), which is extremely useful for application layout. For more information, see [Attached Properties Overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/properties/attached-properties-overview).
## Derived Panel Elements
Many objects derive from [Panel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.panel), but not all of them are intended for use as root layout providers. There are six defined panel classes ([Canvas](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.canvas), [DockPanel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.dockpanel), [Grid](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.grid), [StackPanel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.stackpanel), [VirtualizingStackPanel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.virtualizingstackpanel), and [WrapPanel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.wrappanel)) that are designed specifically for creating application UI.
Each panel element encapsulates its own special functionality, as seen in the following table.

## User Interface Panels
There are six panel classes available in WPF that are optimized to support UI scenarios: [Canvas](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.canvas), [DockPanel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.dockpanel), [Grid](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.grid), [StackPanel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.stackpanel), [VirtualizingStackPanel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.virtualizingstackpanel), and [WrapPanel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.wrappanel). These panel elements are easy to use, versatile, and extensible enough for most applications.
Each derived [Panel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.panel) element treats sizing constraints differently. Understanding how a [Panel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.panel) handles constraints in either the horizontal or vertical direction can make layout more predictable.

### Canvas
The [Canvas](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.canvas) element enables positioning of content according to absolute _x-_ and _y-_ coordinates. Elements can be drawn in a unique location; or, if elements occupy the same coordinates, the order in which they appear in markup determines the order in which the elements are drawn.
[Canvas](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.canvas) provides the most flexible layout support of any [Panel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.panel). Height and Width properties are used to define the area of the canvas, and elements inside are assigned absolute coordinates relative to the area of the parent [Canvas](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.canvas). Four attached properties, [Canvas.Left](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.canvas.left), [Canvas.Top](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.canvas.top), [Canvas.Right](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.canvas.right) and [Canvas.Bottom](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.canvas.bottom), allow fine control of object placement within a [Canvas](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.canvas), allowing the developer to position and arrange elements precisely on the screen.
#### ClipToBounds Within a Canvas
[Canvas](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.canvas) can position child elements at any position on the screen, even at coordinates that are outside of its own defined [Height](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.frameworkelement.height) and [Width](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.frameworkelement.width). Furthermore, [Canvas](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.canvas) is not affected by the size of its children. As a result, it is possible for a child element to overdraw other elements outside the bounding rectangle of the parent [Canvas](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.canvas). The default behavior of a [Canvas](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.canvas) is to allow children to be drawn outside the bounds of the parent [Canvas](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.canvas). If this behavior is undesirable, the [ClipToBounds](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.uielement.cliptobounds) property can be set to `true`. This causes [Canvas](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.canvas) to clip to its own size. [Canvas](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.canvas) is the only layout element that allows children to be drawn outside its bounds.

#### Defining and Using a Canvas
A [Canvas](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.canvas) can be instantiated simply by using Extensible Application Markup Language (XAML) or code. The following example demonstrates how to use [Canvas](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.canvas) to absolutely position content. This code produces three 100-pixel squares. The first square is red, and its top-left (_x, y_) position is specified as (0, 0). The second square is green, and its top-left position is (100, 100), just below and to the right of the first square. The third square is blue, and its top-left position is (50, 50), thus encompassing the lower-right quadrant of the first square and the upper-left quadrant of the second. Because the third square is laid out last, it appears to be on top of the other two squares—that is, the overlapping portions assume the color of the third box.
C# Copy
```

// Create the application's main window
mainWindow = new Window ();
mainWindow.Title = "Canvas Sample";

// Create the Canvas
myParentCanvas = new Canvas();
myParentCanvas.Width = 400;
myParentCanvas.Height = 400;

// Define child Canvas elements
myCanvas1 = new Canvas();
myCanvas1.Background = Brushes.Red;
myCanvas1.Height = 100;
myCanvas1.Width = 100;
Canvas.SetTop(myCanvas1, 0);
Canvas.SetLeft(myCanvas1, 0);

myCanvas2 = new Canvas();
myCanvas2.Background = Brushes.Green;
myCanvas2.Height = 100;
myCanvas2.Width = 100;
Canvas.SetTop(myCanvas2, 100);
Canvas.SetLeft(myCanvas2, 100);

myCanvas3 = new Canvas();
myCanvas3.Background = Brushes.Blue;
myCanvas3.Height = 100;
myCanvas3.Width = 100;
Canvas.SetTop(myCanvas3, 50);
Canvas.SetLeft(myCanvas3, 50);

// Add child elements to the Canvas' Children collection
myParentCanvas.Children.Add(myCanvas1);
myParentCanvas.Children.Add(myCanvas2);
myParentCanvas.Children.Add(myCanvas3);

// Add the parent Canvas as the Content of the Window Object
mainWindow.Content = myParentCanvas;
mainWindow.Show ();


```

### DockPanel
The [DockPanel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.dockpanel) element uses the [DockPanel.Dock](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.dockpanel.dock) attached property as set in child content elements to position content along the edges of a container. When [DockPanel.Dock](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.dockpanel.dock) is set to [Top](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.dock#system-windows-controls-dock-top) or [Bottom](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.dock#system-windows-controls-dock-bottom), it positions child elements above or below each other. When [DockPanel.Dock](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.dockpanel.dock) is set to [Left](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.dock#system-windows-controls-dock-left) or [Right](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.dock#system-windows-controls-dock-right), it positions child elements to the left or right of each other. The [LastChildFill](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.dockpanel.lastchildfill) property determines the position of the final element added as a child of a [DockPanel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.dockpanel).
You can use [DockPanel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.dockpanel) to position a group of related controls, such as a set of buttons. Alternately, you can use it to create a "paned" UI, similar to that found in Microsoft Outlook.
#### Sizing to Content
If its [Height](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.frameworkelement.height) and [Width](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.frameworkelement.width) properties are not specified, [DockPanel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.dockpanel) sizes to its content. The size can increase or decrease to accommodate the size of its child elements. However, when these properties are specified and there is no longer room for the next specified child element, [DockPanel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.dockpanel) does not display that child element or subsequent child elements and does not measure subsequent child elements.
#### LastChildFill
By default, the last child of a [DockPanel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.dockpanel) element will "fill" the remaining, unallocated space. If this behavior is not desired, set the [LastChildFill](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.dockpanel.lastchildfill) property to `false`.
#### Defining and Using a DockPanel
The following example demonstrates how to partition space using a [DockPanel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.dockpanel). Five [Border](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.border) elements are added as children of a parent [DockPanel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.dockpanel). Each uses a different positioning property of a [DockPanel](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.dockpanel) to partition space. The final element "fills" the remaining, unallocated space.
```

// Create the application's main window
mainWindow = gcnew Window();
mainWindow->Title = "DockPanel Sample";

// Create the DockPanel
DockPanel^ myDockPanel = gcnew DockPanel();
myDockPanel->LastChildFill = true;

// Define the child content
Border^ myBorder1 = gcnew Border();
myBorder1->Height = 25;
myBorder1->Background = Brushes::SkyBlue;
myBorder1->BorderBrush = Brushes::Black;
myBorder1->BorderThickness = Thickness(1);
DockPanel::SetDock(myBorder1, Dock::Top);
TextBlock^ myTextBlock1 = gcnew TextBlock();
myTextBlock1->Foreground = Brushes::Black;
myTextBlock1->Text = "Dock = Top";
myBorder1->Child = myTextBlock1;

Border^ myBorder2 = gcnew Border();
myBorder2->Height = 25;
myBorder2->Background = Brushes::SkyBlue;
myBorder2->BorderBrush = Brushes::Black;
myBorder2->BorderThickness = Thickness(1);
DockPanel::SetDock(myBorder2, Dock::Top);
TextBlock^ myTextBlock2 = gcnew TextBlock();
myTextBlock2->Foreground = Brushes::Black;
myTextBlock2->Text = "Dock = Top";
myBorder2->Child = myTextBlock2;

Border^ myBorder3 = gcnew Border();
myBorder3->Height = 25;
myBorder3->Background = Brushes::LemonChiffon;
myBorder3->BorderBrush = Brushes::Black;
myBorder3->BorderThickness = Thickness(1);
DockPanel::SetDock(myBorder3, Dock::Bottom);
TextBlock^ myTextBlock3 = gcnew TextBlock();
myTextBlock3->Foreground = Brushes::Black;
myTextBlock3->Text = "Dock = Bottom";
myBorder3->Child = myTextBlock3;

Border^ myBorder4 = gcnew Border();
myBorder4->Width = 200;
myBorder4->Background = Brushes::PaleGreen;
myBorder4->BorderBrush = Brushes::Black;
myBorder4->BorderThickness = Thickness(1);
DockPanel::SetDock(myBorder4, Dock::Left);
TextBlock^ myTextBlock4 = gcnew TextBlock();
myTextBlock4->Foreground = Brushes::Black;
myTextBlock4->Text = "Dock = Left";
myBorder4->Child = myTextBlock4;

Border^ myBorder5 = gcnew Border();
myBorder5->Background = Brushes::White;
myBorder5->BorderBrush = Brushes::Black;
myBorder5->BorderThickness = Thickness(1);
TextBlock^ myTextBlock5 = gcnew TextBlock();
myTextBlock5->Foreground = Brushes::Black;
myTextBlock5->Text = "This content will Fill the remaining space";

### Grid
The [Grid](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.grid) element merges the functionality of an absolute positioning and tabular data control. A [Grid](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.grid) enables you to easily position and style elements. [Grid](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.grid) allows you to define flexible row and column groupings, and even provides a mechanism to share sizing information between multiple [Grid](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.grid) elements.
#### How is Grid Different from Table
[Table](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.documents.table) and [Grid](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.grid) share some common functionality, but each is best suited for different scenarios. A [Table](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.documents.table) is designed for use within flow content (see [Flow Document Overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/advanced/flow-document-overview) for more information on flow content). Grids are best used inside of forms (basically anywhere outside of flow content). Within a [FlowDocument](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.documents.flowdocument), [Table](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.documents.table) supports flow content behaviors like pagination, column reflow, and content selection while a [Grid](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.grid) does not. A [Grid](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.grid) on the other hand is best used outside of a [FlowDocument](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.documents.flowdocument) for many reasons including [Grid](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.grid) adds elements based on a row and column index, [Table](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.documents.table) does not. The [Grid](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.grid) element allows layering of child content, allowing more than one element to exist within a single "cell." [Table](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.documents.table) does not support layering. Child elements of a [Grid](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.grid) can be absolutely positioned relative to the area of their "cell" boundaries. [Table](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.documents.table) does not support this feature. Finally, a [Grid](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.grid) is lighter weight than a [Table](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.documents.table).
#### Sizing Behavior of Columns and Rows
Columns and rows defined within a [Grid](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.grid) can take advantage of [Star](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.gridunittype#system-windows-gridunittype-star) sizing in order to distribute remaining space proportionally. When [Star](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.gridunittype#system-windows-gridunittype-star) is selected as the Height or Width of a row or column, that column or row receives a weighted proportion of remaining available space. This is in contrast to [Auto](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.gridunittype#system-windows-gridunittype-auto), which will distribute space evenly based on the size of the content within a column or row. This value is expressed as `*` or `2*` when using Extensible Application Markup Language (XAML). In the first case, the row or column would receive one times the available space, in the second case, two times, and so on. By combining this technique to proportionally distribute space with a [HorizontalAlignment](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.frameworkelement.horizontalalignment) and [VerticalAlignment](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.frameworkelement.verticalalignment) value of `Stretch` it is possible to partition layout space by percentage of screen space. [Grid](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.controls.grid) is the only layout panel that can distribute space in this manner.
#### Defining and Using a Grid
The following example demonstrates how to build a UI similar to that found on the Run dialog available on the Windows Start menu.

grid1.Children.Add(txt2);
grid1.Children.Add(tb1);
grid1.Children.Add(button1);
